extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in combinatorics and graph theory (undergraduate/graduate level)
extracted.subtask_description: Formal definitions and conventional terminology for basic graph- and tree-theoretic objects (graphs, digraphs, walks, trees, plane trees, m-ary trees, etc.), together with drawing conventions and related remarks used throughout the textbook.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite graph as a triple (V, E, φ)
rubrics_metrics.description: A finite graph is a triple G = (V, E, φ), where V is a finite set of vertices, E is a finite set of edges, and φ is a function that assigns to each edge e a 2-element multiset of vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If φ(e) = {u, v} then e is considered to join vertices u and v; we say u and v are adjacent and u and e (and v and e) are incident. If u = v then e is called a loop. In practice φ is rarely mentioned explicitly and edges are often written e = uv or identified with the set {u, v}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple graph
rubrics_metrics.description: A graph G is called simple if φ is injective (one-to-one) and has no loops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the simple-graph case it is common to identify each edge with the 2-element set of its endpoints and to omit explicit reference to φ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Walk, closed walk, trail, path, cycle
rubrics_metrics.description: A walk of length n from u to v is a sequence v0 e1 v1 e2 v2 ··· en vn with v0 = u and vn = v and each consecutive vertex and edge incident. A walk is closed if v0 = vn. A trail is a walk whose edges ei are distinct. A path is a walk whose vertices (hence edges) are distinct. If n ≥ 1 and all vi are distinct except v0 = vn, the walk is called a cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: some authors call what is here a 'walk' a 'path'; the book's conventions are stated explicitly. The sequence of vertices alone (v0 v1 ··· vn) suffices in the simple graph case to determine the walk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connected graph
rubrics_metrics.description: A graph is connected if it is nonempty and any two distinct vertices are joined by a path (or walk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard notion of connectedness used throughout the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forest and free tree
rubrics_metrics.description: A graph without cycles is called a free forest or simply a forest. A connected graph without cycles is called a free tree (often just 'a tree').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the unrooted (free) notions; rooted trees are introduced separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digraph (directed graph) convention
rubrics_metrics.description: A digraph is defined analogously to a graph, except φ : E → V × V so that an edge is an ordered pair (u, v) (possibly equal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notions of walk, path, trail, cycle carry over naturally to digraphs; see Section 4.7.1 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rooted tree (recursive definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rooted tree T is a finite set of vertices with: (a) one specially designated vertex called the root, and (b) the remaining vertices partitioned into m ≥ 0 disjoint nonempty sets T1, …, Tm, each of which is a tree (the Ti are called subtrees of the root).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recursive definition specifies the structure of a rooted tree. Subtrees, children/successors, and parent/predecessor follow from this structure; every non-root vertex has a unique parent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parent, child, leaf/endpoint terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: In a rooted tree, a vertex w is a child (successor) of its parent (predecessor) v when w is in one of the subtrees rooted at v. Vertices without children are called leaves or endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example diagrams (Figure 4.33) illustrate these relations and common naming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plane tree (ordered tree)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ordered (plane) tree is obtained by replacing (b) in the rooted-tree definition with: the remaining vertices (excluding the root) are put into an ordered partition (T1, …, Tm) of m ≥ 0 pairwise disjoint nonempty sets, each of which is a plane tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The order (T1, …, Tm) is significant and is depicted left-to-right in drawings. This contrasts with unordered rooted trees that only care about the multiset of subtrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: m-ary tree and binary tree
rubrics_metrics.description: For m ≥ 2 an m-ary tree is defined by: (a'') either T is empty, or else one vertex is designated the root; (b'') the remaining vertices are put into a (weak) ordered partition (T1, …, Tm) of exactly m disjoint (possibly empty) sets, each of which is an m-ary tree. A 2-ary tree is called a binary tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empty subtrees are allowed (hence 'weak' partition), and when drawing small m-ary trees the m edges from a vertex are drawn symmetrically. Examples and counts of nonisomorphic small ternary trees are given (Figure 4.35).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete m-ary tree
rubrics_metrics.description: An m-ary tree is complete if every vertex that is not an endpoint has exactly m children. The unique (up to isomorphism) complete m-ary tree of length ℓ has 1 + m + m^2 + … + m^ℓ vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness is a structural constraint used in counting and enumerative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Length of a tree
rubrics_metrics.description: The length ℓ(T) of a tree T is equal to its length as a poset; i.e., the largest ℓ for which there exists a sequence v0, v1, …, vℓ of vertices with vi a child of vi−1 (so v0 is the root).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aligns tree-theoretic height/depth concepts with poset chain length; used when defining complete m-ary trees of a given length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing rooted tree on a linearly ordered vertex set
rubrics_metrics.description: A rooted tree on a linearly ordered vertex set (such as [n]) is increasing if every path from the root is increasing (with respect to the vertex linear order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This combinatorial restriction is relevant in enumerative contexts where vertex labels carry an order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tree as poset and dual tree
rubrics_metrics.description: A tree may be regarded as a poset by considering its diagram a Hasse diagram; regarded as a poset, a tree has a unique maximal element (the root). A dual tree P is a poset such that the Hasse diagram of the dual poset P* is the diagram of a tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This connects tree concepts with partial-order language and allows talking about dual structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing convention for rooted trees
rubrics_metrics.description: When drawing rooted trees the authors place the root at the top (the prevalent convention among computer scientists and combinatorialists), though other authors may place the root at the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The convention affects diagram interpretation; examples illustrate both root/top placement and plane ordering.
